A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices—A–C in v1 and A–I in v3—are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original hallucination-detection experiments across three datasets and multiple LLMs, including benchmark results, ablations, and the attention-perturbation experiment in Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds model evaluations, comparator results, noise-design experiments, and selective-prediction analyses.

M1.justification: The default algorithm remains activation-noise injection followed by token sampling and uncertainty scoring. v3 adds bounded-Gaussian and zero-mean variants, an SNR-based noise-scaling alternative in Appendix A.3, and combination with shuffled input examples. These are limited procedural extensions. Sharing one noise vector across layers was already present in v1's Algorithm 1; its new explanation does not establish a changed default.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate mathematical reasoning on GSM8K, multiple-choice commonsense QA on CSQA, and context-free factual QA on TriviaQA. The revised sample count, additional model, prompt procedures, and selective-prediction analysis remain within this dataset and task coverage. HaluEval is discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v3 Table 4 extends v1 Table 6's Predictive Entropy, Lexical Similarity, and Semantic Entropy comparisons with EigenScore and selfCheckGPT-NLI, each evaluated with and without noise. Table 7 adds an input-example-shuffling comparator and its combination with model noise. Appendix E additionally compares inference-only dropout against additive noise using generation accuracy, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: The reported TriviaQA count changes from 9,960 unique questions to 18,669 questions. Section 3.2 revises the written labeling rule from a majority of responses being incorrect to an incorrect majority-vote answer. Appendix A changes Mistral prompting to its chat template and its TriviaQA noise magnitude from 0.03 to 0.01. v3 also adds Llama-3.2-3B, all-layer injection at 0.005, and coverage sweeps. Table 2 corrects noise magnitude from 0.05 to 0.07. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 substantially extends the existing ablations with all-layer injection, input-perturbation complementarity, bounded Gaussian versus uniform noise, positive versus zero-mean noise, dropout, and shared versus independent layer noise. New coverage–accuracy and Pareto analyses examine selective prediction and detection–accuracy tradeoffs. The attention-versus-MLP analysis already existed in v1 Appendix C and is retained as v3 Appendix D.

E5.justification: Both versions report Table 3 means and 95% confidence intervals using 25 bootstraps from 40 generated samples, and retain the corresponding bootstrap procedure for Figure 4. Additional rows follow this practice; supplementary comparisons primarily report point estimates. No new seed information, repeated-run procedure, significance testing, or uncertainty-estimation method is introduced.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds Llama-3.2-3B results, including GSM8K AUROC 76.53 without noise and 82.70 with noise. Mistral's GSM8K entries change from 78.06/81.26 to 75.85/78.50 under revised reported settings, so this is not a matched-setting performance decline. Numerous comparator and ablation outcomes are added, including shared versus independent noise at 82.70 versus 80.20 in Table 12. Appendix A.3 replaces the Llama-2-13B constant-noise example with Llama-3.2-3B SNR results.

T1.justification: Section 2 replaces token-level Bayesian averaging with a sequence-level predictive probability containing the product of token probabilities inside the integral. Equation 3 generalizes the uniform perturbation factors to bounded distributions qi, subsequently instantiated as uniform noise. Appendix B's assumption and weight-to-bias derivation remain unchanged; no substantial new proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a simple, training-free perturbation approach that approximates Bayesian model uncertainty and complements token sampling to improve hallucination detection. v3 foregrounds inference-time sampling and compatibility with uncertainty metrics, but these capabilities were already stated or demonstrated in v1. The additional evidence does not materially redefine the core claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations connecting perturbation sensitivity to out-of-distribution detection, shared noise to avoiding cancellation across skip connections, and dropout degradation to disrupted information pathways. It interprets alternative noise distributions as evidence of robustness and introduces calibration and Pareto interpretations of the new analyses. It also explains why dropout-based Bayesian approximations do not naturally apply to many pretrained LLMs.

D1.justification: v3 documents the answer-extraction anchor, BERT-based grouping of free-form answers, the pyvene IntervenableModel interface, batching of independently perturbed samples, and Llama-3.2 layer ranges and noise magnitudes. These expand existing implementation documentation. The PDFs do not establish whether newly described BERT grouping was newly implemented. Hardware and the use of pretrained models without fine-tuning remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially expand positioning against single-response detectors and auxiliary probes, input-perturbation approaches, and out-of-distribution detection. Added works include Kossen et al., Gao et al., Jiang's prompt ensembles, and Liu and Qin's OOD studies. Earlier discussion and citations concerning DoLa, truthfulness intervention, and self-reported confidence are removed or replaced. This exceeds bibliographic updates such as Lin's publication-year change.

P1.justification: The introduction, Bayesian-framework exposition, related work, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Several ablation discussions are condensed, Section 2 is renamed, and the uncertainty-metric ablation moves from Section 4.5 to Section 4.2. Terminology increasingly emphasizes noise-enhanced sampling. These narrative revisions are substantial beyond the accompanying scientific additions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a two-column format to a predominantly single-column ICLR layout, with extensive resizing and repositioning of figures, tables, and Algorithm 1. Existing tables are reformatted or expanded, and the uncertainty-metric comparison is relocated. Five additional tables and two new figures display input perturbation, noise-design comparisons, coverage–accuracy curves, and Pareto results.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens support for the existing method through additional comparators and direct tests of previously unexamined noise choices (Table 4 and Appendices C, H, and I). Figure 5 adds useful evidence for selective prediction, and implementation explanations improve clarity. These extend an already substantial experimental foundation. The overall gain is limited by unreconciled TriviaQA protocol revisions alongside retained scores, and by interpreting coverage–accuracy improvement as calibration, which that analysis alone does not establish.
